speaker: SAM
text: Welcome back to Tech Leadership Unpacked. I'm Sam Rivera. We're in the home stretch - episode nine. Today we're talking about API design, and I'll admit, this might seem deeply technical, but APIs are increasingly a product concern.

speaker: ALEX
text: I'm Alex Chen. Sam's right. If you have external developers, partners, or even internal teams consuming your services, your API is a product. A well-designed API creates leverage - people can build on your platform. A poorly designed API creates friction, support burden, and abandoned integrations.

speaker: SAM
text: So how do we build APIs that developers love?

speaker: ALEX
text: That's exactly what we'll cover. We'll talk principles that apply whether you're building REST, GraphQL, or internal services.

speaker: SAM
text: Let's start with principles. What makes a good API?

speaker: ALEX
text: Several qualities matter.

speaker: ALEX
text: Consistency - the API behaves predictably. If one endpoint returns paginated results with {data: [], pagination: {}}, all endpoints do. If one uses camelCase, all do. Consistency reduces cognitive load.

speaker: SAM
text: That seems obvious. Why does it go wrong?

speaker: ALEX
text: Different teams building different endpoints. No style guide. Rushing to ship. You end up with /users returning {users: []} and /products returning {items: []}. Small inconsistencies multiply into confusion.

speaker: ALEX
text: Intuitiveness - developers can guess how things work. If you know how to list users, you can guess how to list products. Following conventions and patterns makes APIs learnable.

speaker: SAM
text: What conventions matter?

speaker: ALEX
text: Industry standards like REST conventions, HTTP verb semantics, status codes. If your API uses POST for everything and returns 200 for errors, you're fighting expectations.

speaker: ALEX
text: Simplicity - the API does what's needed without unnecessary complexity. Every optional parameter, every configuration flag, every edge case you support has a maintenance cost. Start simple, add complexity only when needed.

speaker: SAM
text: Isn't more flexibility better?

speaker: ALEX
text: Flexibility has costs. More ways to do things means more ways to do things wrong, more documentation needed, more support questions. Opinionated APIs that guide users toward the right path are often better.

speaker: ALEX
text: Evolvability - the API can change without breaking existing users. You'll always need to add features, fix mistakes, evolve the product. Good API design anticipates change.

speaker: SAM
text: How do you design for change?

speaker: ALEX
text: Versioning strategies, additive-only changes, deprecation policies. We'll dig into these.

speaker: ALEX
text: Documentation - this isn't really a property of the API itself, but it's inseparable. An undocumented API barely exists. Documentation is part of the product.

speaker: SAM
text: REST is still the most common API style, right? Let's go deep there.

speaker: ALEX
text: Yes, REST dominates. Let's cover how to do it well.

speaker: ALEX
text: Resources and URLs. REST is resource-oriented. URLs identify resources, not actions. Nouns, not verbs.

speaker: ALEX
text: Good: /users/123 - the user resource

speaker: ALEX
text: Bad: /getUser?id=123 - RPC-style verb in URL

speaker: SAM
text: What about actions like "send email" or "archive"?

speaker: ALEX
text: This is where REST gets tricky. Options:

speaker: ALEX
text: Model as resource state change. Archive a user = PATCH /users/123 with {archived: true}.

speaker: ALEX
text: Model as sub-resource. Send email = POST /users/123/emails.

speaker: ALEX
text: Accept non-RESTful actions for truly action-oriented operations. POST /users/123/send-reminder. Not pure REST, but pragmatic.

speaker: ALEX
text: HTTP Methods. Use them correctly:

speaker: ALEX
text: GET - retrieve data. Must be safe and idempotent - calling it twice shouldn't change anything.

speaker: ALEX
text: POST - create new resources, or perform actions.

speaker: ALEX
text: PUT - replace an entire resource.

speaker: ALEX
text: PATCH - partial update to a resource.

speaker: ALEX
text: DELETE - remove a resource.

speaker: SAM
text: What's the difference between PUT and PATCH in practice?

speaker: ALEX
text: PUT: "Here's the complete new state." You send all fields, missing fields might be set to null.

speaker: ALEX
text: PATCH: "Update these specific fields." You send only what's changing.

speaker: ALEX
text: PATCH is usually what you want for updates. PUT is for complete replacement.

speaker: ALEX
text: Status Codes. Use them meaningfully:

speaker: ALEX
text: 2xx - Success. 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content.

speaker: ALEX
text: 3xx - Redirection. 301, 302 for moved resources.

speaker: ALEX
text: 4xx - Client errors. 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 404 Not Found, 422 Validation Error.

speaker: ALEX
text: 5xx - Server errors. 500 Internal Error, 503 Service Unavailable.

speaker: SAM
text: I've seen APIs that return 200 with error messages in the body.

speaker: ALEX
text: That's an anti-pattern. Status codes exist for a reason. Clients and infrastructure (caches, load balancers, monitoring) rely on them. If you return 200 for errors, retries won't work correctly, caching breaks, and clients can't trust responses.

speaker: ALEX
text: Request and Response Design.

speaker: ALEX
text: Use JSON - it's the standard. Design clear, predictable response structures.

speaker: ALEX
text: Envelope or no envelope? Some APIs wrap everything: {data: {}, meta: {}}. Others return data directly. Both work; pick one and be consistent.

speaker: SAM
text: What about errors?

speaker: ALEX
text: Errors should be structured and helpful:

speaker: ALEX
text: ```json

speaker: ALEX
text: "error": {

speaker: ALEX
text: "code": "VALIDATION_FAILED",

speaker: ALEX
text: "message": "Email is invalid",

speaker: ALEX
text: "details": [

speaker: ALEX
text: {"field": "email", "issue": "must be a valid email address"}

speaker: ALEX
text: Machine-readable codes for programmatic handling. Human-readable messages for debugging. Details for complex errors.

speaker: SAM
text: List endpoints seem straightforward but can get complex. How do you handle pagination?

speaker: ALEX
text: Several patterns:

speaker: ALEX
text: Offset pagination. ?offset=20&limit=10 - skip 20, get 10. Simple, but has problems: skipping millions of rows is expensive, and pages shift if items are added/removed.

speaker: ALEX
text: Page-based. ?page=3&per_page=10 - similar issues to offset, just different parameters.

speaker: ALEX
text: Cursor-based. ?cursor=abc123&limit=10 - the cursor is an opaque pointer to a position. Fast for any position, stable if items change. Preferred for large datasets or real-time data.

speaker: SAM
text: How do you implement cursor pagination?

speaker: ALEX
text: The cursor encodes position - often the ID or timestamp of the last item. "Give me 10 items after this one." The response includes the next cursor. Client uses it for the next page.

speaker: SAM
text: What about filtering?

speaker: ALEX
text: Several approaches:

speaker: ALEX
text: Query parameters. ?status=active&type=admin - simple key-value filters.

speaker: ALEX
text: Filter parameter. ?filter[status]=active&filter[created_after]=2023-01-01 - namespaced filters.

speaker: ALEX
text: Query language. ?filter=status:active AND created>2023-01-01 - powerful but complex.

speaker: ALEX
text: Start simple. Elaborate query languages are rarely worth the complexity unless you're building a search API.

speaker: SAM
text: And sorting?

speaker: ALEX
text: Common patterns:

speaker: ALEX
text: ?sort=created_at - ascending by created_at

speaker: ALEX
text: ?sort=-created_at - descending (dash prefix)

speaker: ALEX
text: ?sort=status,-created_at - multiple fields

speaker: ALEX
text: Be explicit about defaults. Document what's sortable - not everything should be.

speaker: SAM
text: What about including related data?

speaker: ALEX
text: This is a big topic. Options:

speaker: ALEX
text: Nested data. Include related data in the response: user includes their posts.

speaker: ALEX
text: Links. Provide URLs to related resources: {"posts_url": "/users/123/posts"}.

speaker: ALEX
text: Sparse fieldsets. ?fields=id,name,email - return only requested fields.

speaker: ALEX
text: Include parameter. ?include=posts,comments - embed related resources.

speaker: ALEX
text: Trade-offs: nested data is convenient but can be huge. Separate requests add latency. Choose based on typical use cases.

speaker: SAM
text: REST isn't the only option. What about GraphQL?

speaker: ALEX
text: GraphQL is a query language for APIs. Instead of fixed endpoints returning fixed shapes, clients request exactly what they need.

speaker: SAM
text: Example?

speaker: ALEX
text: Client sends:

speaker: ALEX
text: ```graphql

speaker: ALEX
text: query {

speaker: ALEX
text: user(id: "123") {

speaker: ALEX
text: name

speaker: ALEX
text: email

speaker: ALEX
text: posts(first: 5) {

speaker: ALEX
text: title

speaker: ALEX
text: publishedAt

speaker: ALEX
text: Server returns exactly that shape. No over-fetching (getting data you don't need) or under-fetching (needing multiple requests).

speaker: SAM
text: When does GraphQL make sense?

speaker: ALEX
text: Strong use cases:

speaker: ALEX
text: Diverse clients with different needs. Mobile wants minimal data, web wants more, admin wants everything.

speaker: ALEX
text: Complex, interconnected data. Graph-like relationships where REST gets awkward.

speaker: ALEX
text: Rapid frontend iteration. Frontend can change data requirements without backend changes.

speaker: SAM
text: What are the downsides?

speaker: ALEX
text: Complexity. Setting up a GraphQL server is more involved than REST. Schema definition, resolvers, tooling.

speaker: ALEX
text: Caching is harder. HTTP caching works great with REST. GraphQL's variable queries make standard caching tricky.

speaker: ALEX
text: N+1 query problems. Naive implementations can generate many database queries. Need dataloader patterns.

speaker: ALEX
text: Security concerns. Clients can request deeply nested queries that overload the server. Need query complexity limits.

speaker: SAM
text: So when would you choose REST over GraphQL?

speaker: ALEX
text: Simple CRUD APIs. Public APIs where documentation and simplicity matter. Cases where HTTP caching is important. When the team doesn't have GraphQL expertise.

speaker: SAM
text: What about gRPC?

speaker: ALEX
text: gRPC is a high-performance RPC framework using Protocol Buffers. Binary format, schema-first, code generation, streaming support.

speaker: ALEX
text: Good for: internal service-to-service communication, low-latency requirements, polyglot environments where generated clients help.

speaker: ALEX
text: Less good for: browser clients (though possible with gRPC-web), public APIs where JSON is expected.

speaker: SAM
text: Any guidance on choosing?

speaker: ALEX
text: My defaults:

speaker: ALEX
text: Public APIs → REST. Widest compatibility, simplest tooling.

speaker: ALEX
text: Client-driven needs, complex data → GraphQL.

speaker: ALEX
text: Internal services, performance-critical → gRPC.

speaker: ALEX
text: But context matters. Use what your team knows and what fits the problem.

speaker: SAM
text: How do you handle API changes over time?

speaker: ALEX
text: This is one of the hardest parts of API design. Once an API is in use, changing it is painful.

speaker: ALEX
text: First principle: Prefer additive, non-breaking changes. Add new fields, new endpoints, new parameters. Don't remove or rename existing ones.

speaker: SAM
text: What counts as a breaking change?

speaker: ALEX
text: Removing or renaming fields. Changing field types. Changing required/optional status. Changing response structure. Removing endpoints. Changing error formats.

speaker: SAM
text: How do you handle breaking changes when you need them?

speaker: ALEX
text: Versioning. Common strategies:

speaker: ALEX
text: URL versioning. /v1/users, /v2/users. Clear, cacheable, but ugly URLs and harder to migrate incrementally.

speaker: ALEX
text: Header versioning. Accept: application/vnd.api+json; version=2. Cleaner URLs but less visible, harder to test.

speaker: ALEX
text: Query parameter. ?api_version=2. Simple but not RESTful.

speaker: SAM
text: Which do you prefer?

speaker: ALEX
text: URL versioning for clarity, especially for public APIs. Internal APIs can use headers or content negotiation.

speaker: ALEX
text: Deprecation policies are critical. When you version:

speaker: ALEX
text: 1. Announce deprecation with timeline

speaker: ALEX
text: 2. Add deprecation headers to old version responses

speaker: ALEX
text: 3. Provide migration guide

speaker: ALEX
text: 4. Monitor usage of old version

speaker: ALEX
text: 5. Sunset when usage is low enough

speaker: SAM
text: How long should you support old versions?

speaker: ALEX
text: Depends on your users. Internal APIs can move faster. Public APIs with enterprise customers might need years. Set expectations upfront and stick to them.

speaker: ALEX
text: Compatibility strategies:

speaker: ALEX
text: Request compatibility. Accept old and new request formats. Convert internally.

speaker: ALEX
text: Response compatibility. Return new fields alongside old ones. Clients can migrate gradually.

speaker: SAM
text: What about field defaults?

speaker: ALEX
text: Tricky area. If you add a required field to a creation request, that's breaking. Solutions: make new fields optional with defaults, or gate behind feature flags or versions.

speaker: SAM
text: We have a whole episode on security, but let's touch on API-specific concerns.

speaker: ALEX
text: Key considerations:

speaker: ALEX
text: Authentication patterns.

speaker: ALEX
text: API Keys - simple, good for server-to-server. Pass in header (not URL - URLs get logged). Easy to revoke.

speaker: ALEX
text: OAuth 2.0 - standard for delegated authorization. User grants app permission. Tokens have scopes. Refresh tokens for long-lived sessions.

speaker: ALEX
text: JWTs - JSON Web Tokens. Self-contained tokens with claims. Verify signature, no database lookup needed. But revocation is tricky.

speaker: SAM
text: Which should we use?

speaker: ALEX
text: API keys for simple integrations, especially internal. OAuth for user authorization, especially if third parties access user data. JWTs often paired with OAuth as the token format.

speaker: ALEX
text: Authorization - who can do what:

speaker: ALEX
text: RBAC - Role-Based Access Control. Users have roles, roles have permissions.

speaker: ALEX
text: ABAC - Attribute-Based Access Control. Policies based on attributes of user, resource, environment.

speaker: ALEX
text: Resource-level permissions - can this user access this specific resource?

speaker: ALEX
text: Return 403 Forbidden for authorization failures, 401 Unauthorized for authentication failures.

speaker: ALEX
text: Rate limiting - prevent abuse:

speaker: ALEX
text: - Limit by API key, user, IP

speaker: ALEX
text: - Return 429 Too Many Requests

speaker: ALEX
text: - Include retry-after headers

speaker: ALEX
text: - Provide clear documentation of limits

speaker: ALEX
text: HTTPS everywhere. No exceptions. API keys and tokens over HTTP are exposed. HSTS headers to enforce.

speaker: SAM
text: What about input validation?

speaker: ALEX
text: Validate everything. Type checking, length limits, allowed values. Return clear validation errors. Never trust client input. This prevents security issues and improves developer experience.

speaker: SAM
text: Let's talk about documentation. You said it's part of the product.

speaker: ALEX
text: Maybe the most important part for external APIs. Good docs = adoption. Bad docs = support tickets.

speaker: ALEX
text: What to document:

speaker: ALEX
text: Getting started - quick path to first successful call. Authentication, hello world example.

speaker: ALEX
text: Authentication - how to get credentials, how to use them.

speaker: ALEX
text: Reference - every endpoint, request format, response format.

speaker: ALEX
text: Guides - how to accomplish common tasks, workflows.

speaker: ALEX
text: Examples - code samples in multiple languages.

speaker: ALEX
text: Errors - every error code, what causes it, how to fix.

speaker: ALEX
text: Changelog - what changed in each version.

speaker: SAM
text: What tools are standard?

speaker: ALEX
text: OpenAPI (Swagger) - spec for describing REST APIs. Tools generate docs, SDKs, mocks from the spec.

speaker: ALEX
text: Redoc, Slate, ReadMe - documentation platforms.

speaker: ALEX
text: Postman - collections for interactive testing and documentation.

speaker: SAM
text: Should we generate SDKs?

speaker: ALEX
text: For major platforms - JavaScript, Python, Ruby, Go - SDKs dramatically improve developer experience. Generated from OpenAPI or hand-crafted for polish.

speaker: ALEX
text: Interactive documentation is powerful. Try-it-out features in docs let developers experiment without writing code. Reduces time to first successful call.

speaker: SAM
text: What makes documentation great?

speaker: ALEX
text: Clear, concise writing. Realistic examples. Good search. Up-to-date with the actual API. Version-matched. Quick path to solving real problems.

speaker: ALEX
text: Developer experience (DX) goes beyond docs:

speaker: ALEX
text: - Sandbox environments for testing

speaker: ALEX
text: - Webhook testing tools

speaker: ALEX
text: - CLI tools for common operations

speaker: ALEX
text: - Clear error messages that guide solutions

speaker: ALEX
text: - Responsive support channels

speaker: ALEX
text: - Status pages for API health

speaker: SAM
text: Let's summarize. What should product leaders know about API design?

speaker: ALEX
text: APIs are products. They have users, they need design, they need documentation, they need support. Treat them with the same rigor as your customer-facing product.

speaker: SAM
text: Who should own API design?

speaker: ALEX
text: Joint ownership between product (what capabilities to expose) and engineering (how to expose them well). For public APIs, consider a dedicated API product manager.

speaker: ALEX
text: Consistency over perfection. A consistent API is better than a perfect one. Establish patterns early, document them, enforce them in code review.

speaker: ALEX
text: Plan for evolution. You will make mistakes. You will need to add features. Design for change with versioning, deprecation policies, and additive changes.

speaker: ALEX
text: Invest in developer experience. Time spent on docs, SDKs, and examples pays back in adoption, reduced support, and developer goodwill.

speaker: SAM
text: Any anti-patterns to avoid?

speaker: ALEX
text: Exposing internal implementation. Your API should model the domain, not your database schema.

speaker: ALEX
text: Breaking changes without warning. Erodes trust permanently.

speaker: ALEX
text: Inconsistent response formats. Makes integration fragile.

speaker: ALEX
text: Missing error details. "Something went wrong" is not helpful.

speaker: ALEX
text: No rate limiting. Invites abuse and cascading failures.

speaker: SAM
text: One thing to remember?

speaker: ALEX
text: Think of your API from the consumer's perspective. Every design decision should make their life easier. If you wouldn't want to use your own API, redesign it.

speaker: SAM
text: Perfect. Final episode coming up: Security and Development Methodologies. How to build securely and deliver effectively.

speaker: ALEX
text: The grand finale.
